Unraveling the Kagome Antiferromagnetic 3​J3J Model and Its Materials: An Integrated Approach

September 10, 2026
Abstract

We investigate the ground-state and finite-temperature properties of the kagome antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model with three inequivalent couplings, dubbed the 3​J3J model, which is designed for the candidate Dirac quantum spin liquid (QSL) material YCu3(OH)6Br2[Br1-x(OH)x] [109]. Employing large-scale density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) supplemented by neural quantum states (NQS) simulations, we identify an intermediate QSL phase between two magnetically ordered phases. We also find that this QSL is separated from the kagome spin liquid ground state at the isotropic limit. To establish a direct comparison with experiments, we compute the specific heat of the model by means of advanced exponential (XTRG) and tangent-space (tanTRG) thermal tensor-network methods. In the magnetically ordered phase, the specific heat over temperature exhibits a shoulder at a temperature that is a fraction of the coupling strength J⎔J_{\hexagon}, which disappears in the QSL phase. These universal behaviors are consistent with the experimentally observed specific heat in 3​J3J materials for both ordered and QSL candidate samples. Our work thus connects microscopic models with experimentally measurable signatures, exemplifying an integrated approach [70] to understanding QSL phenomena in frustrated quantum magnets, with 3​J3J materials serving as a representative case and providing a foundation for future studies.

Introduction.– Quantum magnets provide a fertile ground for exploring exotic quantum phases, among which quantum spin liquids (QSLs) [84, 7, 59, 11, 70, 106] are particularly intriguing and elusive due to their departure from conventional ordered states. Rather than developing conventional long-range order, QSLs can host long-range quantum entanglement, fractionalized excitations, and emergent gauge structures, providing a natural setting for quantum phases beyond the Landau paradigm of symmetry breaking. One promising platform for realizing QSLs is the highly frustrated spin-1/21/2 kagome antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model [37, 41, 114, 112, 48, 58, 27, 113]. Despite extensive numerical and theoretical efforts, however, the nature of its ground state remains debated, with various studies supporting competing scenarios, e.g., a gapped QSL [51, 107, 22, 52, 71, 32, 64, 69, 93], a gapless QSL [77, 46, 47, 49, 44, 38, 66, 53] or valence-bond crystal (VBC) states [12, 90, 13, 24]. This theoretical ambiguity is compounded by experimental challenges: disorder and magnetic impurities in candidate kagome materials [20, 28, 45, 35, 29, 36, 57, 25, 101, 26, 30, 102, 74] can mask intrinsic signatures of QSLs in thermodynamic and spectroscopic measurements and, in some cases, may destabilize the underlying quantum phase.

Recent experimental advances in kagome antiferromagnetic compounds YCu3(OH)6+xX3-x (X=Cl or Br) [63, 109, 108, 67, 105, 34, 111, 65, 94, 16, 3] have opened a promising avenue toward realizing a Dirac QSL with gapless Dirac excitations [84, 7]. Rather than forming an isotropic kagome lattice, these materials exhibit a weakly distorted kagome geometry with three inequivalent nearest-neighbor couplings, J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, and J⎔J_{\hexagon}, defining the so-called 3​J3J model, as illustrated in the inset of Fig. 1. This distortion originates from the displacement of Y3+ ions out of the kagome plane by the polar (OH)- ligand, which splits the uniform hexagon coupling into two alternating couplings, J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} [67, 105]. Experiments on candidate 3​J3J materials have revealed the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phase [94, 16] and provided evidence for a possible Dirac QSL from specific-heat [108, 65, 94] and inelastic neutron scattering [109, 34] measurements. Despite these experimental indications, theoretical understanding of the 3​J3J model remains at an early stage. While the classical phase diagram has been established [40] and recent simulations have provided only a preliminary characterization of the excitation spectrum, with agreement with experiment largely limited to the high-energy regime [34]. More fundamentally, unbiased numerical simulations of the phase diagram of the 3​J3J model, particularly the nature and stability of the putative QSL, is still largely absent. This leaves several essential questions unresolved: Does the QSL survive in the presence of the bond anisotropy intrinsic to the 3​J3J model? How does it relate to the kagome spin liquid (KSL) of the isotropic (1​J1J) model? Do they represent the same quantum phase, or does the bond anisotropy stabilize a distinct QSL? How does it evolve into the neighboring (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases? Moreover, a systematic understanding of its finite-temperature properties and their connection to experimental observations remains elusive. Addressing these questions is essential for establishing whether the 3​J3J model can provide a robust theoretical framework for the experimentally observed QSL phenomena.

Motivated by the integrated strategy [70], in this Letter we combine four state-of-the-art quantum many-body computational approaches with measurements on multiple experimental samples to investigate the kagome antiferromagnetic 3​J3J model, providing a concrete demonstration of the strength of such an integrated strategy. Rather than relying on any single numerical method or experimental signature, we establish the ground-state phase diagram via complementary large-scale density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [103, 104, 87, 88] and neural quantum states (NQS) [15, 61, 82, 99] calculations, characterize the finite-temperature behavior using advanced exponential (XTRG) [18] and tangent-space (tanTRG) [62] thermal tensor-network methods, and compare the resulting numerical predictions against specific-heat measurements from multiple samples, represented by the ordered Y3Cu9(OH)19Cl8 [94] and QSL candidate materials YCu3(OH)6Br2[Br1-x(OH)x] [109, 108, 105] and LuCu3(OH)6Br2[Brx(OH)1-x] [65] samples.

This combined strategy not only allows us to exploit the respective strengths of different numerical approaches using experiment as an independent touchstone, but also enables us to cross-validate and synthesize their insights to uncover the emergent physics of the 3​J3J model beyond the reach of any single method. In particular, it provides an unbiased route to establishing the quantum phase diagram, suggests a gapless intermediate QSL phase, and clarifying its connection to neighboring ordered phases and the experimentally observed finite-temperature behavior.

Model and Method.– The Hamiltonian of kagome antiferromagnetic 3​J3J model is

H=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩1𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨i,j⟩2𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J⎔​∑⟨i,j⟩⎔𝐒i⋅𝐒j,H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle_{1}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle_{2}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{\hexagon}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle_{\hexagon}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}, (1)

where 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i} denotes the spin-1/21/2 operator at site ii (white dots in the inset of Fig. 1). All three couplings are antiferromagnetic, J1,J2,J⎔>0J_{1},J_{2},J_{\hexagon}>0, and correspond to nearest-neighbor interactions. To determine its ground-state phase diagram, we employ complementary approaches based on DMRG and NQS. We set J⎔=1J_{\hexagon}=1 as the energy unit and focus on the parameter regime J1,J2∈[0,1]J_{1},J_{2}\in[0,1]. For the DMRG calculations, we consider YC cylindrical geometries with a fixed circumference of Ly=3L_{y}=3 (YC6) and system lengths Lx=6L_{x}=6, 1212 and 2424, compatible with the 27-site magnetic unit cell of the 3​J3J model. These correspond to total spin numbers N=3×Lx×Ly=54N=3\times L_{x}\times L_{y}=54, 108108 and 216216, respectively. We keep the maximum bond dimension up to D=15,000D=15,000 with U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry implemented, achieving well-converged results with truncation errors below 1.0×10−81.0\times{10}^{-8}. For the NQS calculations, we adopt a Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture with factored attention [98, 99, 79], implemented in two variants that differ in their enforcement of translation symmetry. On the J1=1J_{1}=1 line, the network enforces the full translation symmetry of the 3​J3J Hamiltonian, while on the J1=0.5J_{1}=0.5 line it enforces translation symmetry at the level of a 3×33\times 3 supercell of kagome unit cells, which allows for the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) magnetic order found in the classical phase diagram [40] [see Fig. S5 of the SM [89]]. These simulations are performed on an N=3×6×6N=3\times 6\times 6 system with periodic boundary conditions, and the network parameters are optimized by variational Monte Carlo [9] using the NetKet library [97, 14, 10, 39]. For finite-temperature properties, we employ the advanced tensor-network methods XTRG and tanTRG as complementary approaches for cross-validation. Both methods are applied to YC6 cylinders with a maximum bond dimension of D=2000D=2000, which yields well-converged results. Further technical details of the algorithms are provided in the Supplemental Material (SM) [89].

Phase Diagram.– Our ground-state results for the 3​J3J model obtained from DMRG and NQS calculations are summarized in the phase diagram Fig. 1, where J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} are varied with J⎔=1J_{\hexagon}=1 fixed. We identify a candidate QSL phase (light-blue region) sandwiched between two (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases [40] (light-pink regions). Compared with the classical phase boundaries (gray solid lines) determined by classical Monte Carlo calculations [40], the QSL region is reduced in the large-J1,2J_{1,2} regimes due to enhanced quantum fluctuations. Moreover, it is concentrated around the diagonal symmetry axis J1=J2J_{1}=J_{2}, where the competing interactions are more balanced in strength, favoring the emergence of the QSL. Notably, we have evidence that this QSL phase is separated from the KSL ground state (light-purple regime) in the vicinity of the isotropic 1​J1J model by a phase transition. These results imply that distorted kagome 3​J3J materials are likely to host two distinct QSL phases.

We characterize these distinct quantum phases by examining the static spin structure factor S⁡(𝐤)=(1/N)​∑i,j⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩​ei​𝐤⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)S(\mathbf{k})=(1/N)\sum_{i,j}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}. In the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases, S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) show Bragg peaks at either the 𝐊1\mathbf{K}_{1} points [cf. Fig. 2(a)] or the 𝐊2\mathbf{K}_{2} points [cf. Fig. 2(b)]. It is worth pointing out that these two (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases are physically equivalent, as both correspond to the same ordering wave vector 𝐐=(1/3,1/3)\mathbf{Q}=(1/3,1/3). The apparent distinction between 𝐊1\mathbf{K}_{1} and 𝐊2\mathbf{K}_{2} arises from a transformation that effectively swaps J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} in the Hamiltonian. In stark contrast, the QSL phase exhibits no sharp Bragg peaks in S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) [cf. Fig. 2(c)], but rather a broad and featureless distribution, reflecting the absence of long-range magnetic order. For comparison, we also present S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) for the KSL phase in Fig. 2(d), which likewise exhibits obvious disordered behavior. However, the topology of S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) in these two spin liquid phases differs significantly: S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) is discontinuous at 𝐌2{\mathbf{M}}_{2} points in the QSL phase, whereas it remains continuous at both 𝐌1{\mathbf{M}}_{1} and 𝐌2{\mathbf{M}}_{2} points in the KSL phase. We have verified this distinction across all parameter points within both the QSL and KSL regimes. On the other hand, the real-space spin correlations provide another clear distinction between the QSL and KSL phases. In the QSL phase, the spin correlations decay algebraically as a power law, consistent with the behavior expected for a Dirac QSL state, whereas those in the KSL phase decay exponentially. Further details can be found in the SM [89].

To accurately locate the phase boundaries, we track the evolution of S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) with J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} at the ordering momenta 𝐊1\mathbf{K}_{1} and 𝐊2\mathbf{K}_{2}. As a representative cut through the phase diagram, we fix J1=0.5J_{1}=0.5 and vary J2J_{2}, thereby traversing the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered and QSL phases [cf. Fig. 3(a)]. As J2J_{2} increases, the dominant S⁡(𝐊1)S(\mathbf{K}_{1}) is gradually suppressed. Around J2≃0.35J_{2}\simeq 0.35, it exhibits a pronounced kink, accompanied by the gradual development of S⁡(𝐊2)S(\mathbf{K}_{2}), signaling a phase transition. In the intermediate regime 0.35<J2<0.60.35<J_{2}<0.6, neither S⁡(𝐊1)S(\mathbf{K}_{1}) nor S⁡(𝐊2)S(\mathbf{K}_{2}) dominates, and both magnetic correlations are substantially suppressed, supporting the presence of a QSL phase. Upon further increasing J2J_{2}, S⁡(𝐊1)S(\mathbf{K}_{1}) is completely suppressed near J2≃0.6J_{2}\simeq 0.6, while S⁡(𝐊2)S(\mathbf{K}_{2}) develops a pronounced kink and becomes the dominant magnetic ordering tendency. Since the computational cost of DMRG grows exponentially with cylinder width LyL_{y}, we use NQS as a complementary approach to access wider systems on a torus with Ly=6L_{y}=6 [Fig. 3(b)]. Remarkably, the locations of the transition points remain stable against finite-size effects and boundary conditions, further supporting the robustness of the identified phase boundaries. In Fig. 3(c), we also show the evolution of the entanglement entropy SE​(x)=−Tr⁡[ρx​ln⁡ρx]S_{E}(x)=-\mathrm{Tr}\left[\rho_{x}\ln\rho_{x}\right] from DMRG at the middle of the cylinders x=Lx/2x=L_{x}/2, where ρx\rho_{x} is the reduced density matrix of the subsystem with rung number xx. Two kinks are clearly observed, whose locations are also consistent with those identified from Figs. 3(a-b). Moreover, the entanglement entropy is larger in the ordered phase, consistent with the expected contribution from Goldstone modes [4]. Additionally, we characterize the QSL–KSL transition by tracking the evolution of S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) at 𝐌1\mathbf{M}_{1} and 𝐌2\mathbf{M}_{2} along a cut with fixed J1=1J_{1}=1. Beyond the distinct S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) profiles shown in Figs. 2(c,d), the QSL–KSL transition is signaled by pronounced kinks in S⁡(𝐌1)S(\mathbf{M}_{1}) and S⁡(𝐌2)S(\mathbf{M}_{2}) near J2≃0.94J_{2}\simeq 0.94 [cf. Figs. 3(d,e)], accompanied by singular behavior in SE​(x)S_{E}(x) [cf. Fig. 3(f)]. As an additional cross-check of the phase boundaries, we examine the evolution of S⁡(𝐌)S(\mathbf{M}) in the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases and S⁡(𝐊)S(\mathbf{K}) in the QSL and KSL phases in the SM [89]. The transition points extracted from these independent diagnostics are in excellent agreement.

Finally, to further examine whether the ground state may host VBC states, we also analyze the bond energies across the phase diagram. In both the QSL and KSL phases, we find no discernible signatures of lattice-symmetry breaking, further ruling out VBC as the underlying ground-state order in these regimes [cf. Fig. S4 in the SM [89]].

Specific Heat.– To establish a direct connection between the ground states and experimentally accessible thermal signatures, we calculate the specific heat using XTRG and tanTRG, and present the results as Cv/TC_{v}/T. We consider four representative parameter sets spanning the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered and QSL phases: (J1,J2)=(0.8,0.3)​J⎔(J_{1},J_{2})=(0.8,0.3)J_{\hexagon} and (1,0.4)​J⎔(1,0.4)J_{\hexagon} in the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phase; (0.8,0.75)​J⎔(0.8,0.75)J_{\hexagon} and (1,0.85)​J⎔(1,0.85)J_{\hexagon} in the QSL phase. The corresponding numerical results are shown in Figs. 4(a-b), with the temperature scale set by J⎔=63J_{\hexagon}=63 K following the experimental estimate [50]. We compare these results with experimental data for the ordered material Y3Cu9(OH)19Cl8 [cf. Fig. 4(c)] and three candidate QSL materials, including LuCu3(OH)6Br2[Brx(OH)1-x], YCu3(OH)6O1/3Cl8/3), and YCu3(OH)6Br2[Brx(OH)1-x] [cf. Fig. 4(d)]. We note that the experimental Cv/TC_{v}/T data contain a nonmagnetic phonon contribution that is difficult to subtract reliably at low temperatures, especially below 2525 K. Despite this limitation, the experimental data exhibit clear temperature-dependent features that allow a meaningful comparison with our numerical results, revealing two distinct thermal signatures that differentiate the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3)-ordered and QSL phases.

First, the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phase exhibits a shoulder-like anomaly in Cv/TC_{v}/T at T∼10T\sim 10–2222 K (red shading), which is absent in the QSL phase. This shoulder consistently appears around T∼15T\sim 15 K in the ordered compound Y3Cu9(OH)19Cl8, but is absent in all three candidate QSL materials. This difference suggests that the shoulder serves as a signature of the zero-temperature magnetic order and thus provides a thermal diagnostic for distinguishing the two phases. Second, at T∼5T\sim 5 K (green shading), Cv/TC_{v}/T in the ordered phase exhibits a pronounced minimum, reaching ∼0.1\sim 0.1, while it remains larger (∼0.2\sim 0.2) in the QSL phase. The experimental data show the same trend, with a deep low-temperature dip in the ordered compound and enhanced Cv/TC_{v}/T in the QSL candidates. This enhancement implies a larger low-energy density of states in the QSL phase, which naturally accounts for the stronger low-temperature contribution.

Moreover, in Fig. 5(a), we compare XTRG and tanTRG in the QSL phase at (J1,J2)=(1,0.9)​J⎔(J_{1},J_{2})=(1,0.9)J_{\hexagon} with bond dimensions up to D=2000D=2000 to assess the robustness of our numerical results. The XTRG results are well converged for D=1000D=1000 and 20002000 over the entire temperature range T/J⎔∈[0.05,10]T/J_{\hexagon}\in[0.05,10]. In contrast, tanTRG exhibits pronounced DD dependence at low temperatures, converging to the XTRG results only as DD increases. This confirms the different performance of XTRG and tanTRG and supports the reliability of the results in Figs. 4(a-b). On the other hand, we also compare our XTRG results at the isotropic 1​J1J kagome limit with SPINPACK data from Ref. [86] [cf. Fig. 5(b)]. The good agreement further validates our approach. Finally, to highlight the distinct thermal behavior, we compare Cv/NC_{v}/N at (J1,J2)=(1.0,0.9)​J⎔(J_{1},J_{2})=(1.0,0.9)J_{\hexagon} with that of the 1​J1J model. The QSL-phase data exhibit a prominent shoulder around T/J⎔∼0.1T/J_{\hexagon}\sim 0.1, whereas the 1​J1J model decreases monotonically and smoothly over the same range. This striking difference corroborates our ground-state phase diagram analysis, providing strong evidence that the QSL phase of the 3​J3J model is not adiabatically connected to the 1​J1J limit.

Summary and Discussion.– In this work, we have established the ground-state and finite-temperature properties of the kagome antiferromagnetic 3​J3J model through an integrated investigation, combining two complementary ground-state methods (DMRG and NQS), two finite-temperature tensor-network approaches (XTRG and tanTRG), and experimental specific-heat data from four 3​J3J materials. These independent approaches consistently identify an intermediate QSL phase between two (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases and establish that it is distinct from the KSL phase at the isotropic 1​J1J limit. The consistency between DMRG and NQS results, despite their different geometries and effective system sizes, mitigates uncertainties associated with boundary conditions and finite-size effects, rendering the identification of the QSL phase particularly robust and compelling. The rich quantum phase diagram also highlights the intricate physics arising from the interplay of inequivalent exchange couplings. The calculated specific heat further captures the characteristic shoulder in the ordered regime and its disappearance in the QSL regime, in close agreement with experiments on both ordered and QSL samples.

Beyond establishing the phase diagram and finite-temperature signatures, our integrated analysis also raises several important questions concerning the low-energy physics of the QSL phase. Resolving the corresponding low-energy Dirac-cone structure in the excitation spectrum using both analytic [85] and numerical [43, 54, 42, 23] approaches would provide a more direct characterization of its underlying field theory. On the experimental side, we note that our thermal measurements have not yet accessed a sufficiently low-temperature regime to resolve the T2T^{2} specific heat (Cv∝T2C_{v}\propto T^{2}) expected for a Dirac QSL [91, 33, 77]. Accessing this regime numerically will require further advances in finite-temperature numerical methods to enable reliable simulations at lower temperatures. Besides, the magnetic field response [6, 91, 56] of the 3​J3J model also warrants investigation, including the intriguing 1/91/9 magnetization plateau and quantum oscillations observed therein [110, 60, 55, 111, 50], as well as possible field-induced phase transitions, which may provide further insight into the QSL-KSL transition and offer additional probes of the underlying low-energy theory.

In parallel, NQS have demonstrated their ability to accurately capture ground states, low-lying excitations, and phase boundaries in frustrated magnets, including the square- and triangular-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} models [83, 73] and the Shastry-Sutherland model [99, 72, 75]. Recent studies using variational wave functions based on the transformer architecture have reached periodic clusters of several hundred to more than a thousand spins on the square and triangular lattices [80, 100], and have enabled controlled finite-size extrapolations of energies and order parameters  [100]. The 3​J3J model thus provides a natural yet more demanding setting for such scaling efforts. Its enlarged unit cell and inequivalent exchange couplings lead to a richer low-energy spectrum and substantially more intricate momentum-space structure, while its close connection to experimentally accessible materials makes quantitative theoretical predictions especially valuable. Extending NQS to larger kagome clusters [76], excited-state spectra, and finite-temperature observables such as the specific heat could therefore offer an independent route to the low-energy and thermodynamic properties of the 3​J3J model, complementary to conventional tensor-network approaches.

Supplemental Materials for: “Unraveling the Kagome Antiferromagnetic 3​J3J Model and Its Materials: An Integrated Approach”

In the Supplemental Material, we provide additional results and methodological details supporting the conclusions presented in the main text. In Sec. I, we present additional ground-state results from DMRG and NQS calculations, including the evolution of the static spin structure factor, real-space spin correlations, and bond energies across the phase diagram. In Sec. II, we describe the algorithmic framework and implementation details of the NQS approach used to obtain the ground states. In Sec. III, we provide further technical details of the XTRG and tanTRG thermal tensor-network algorithms, together with the specific heat results for additional parameter points.

I Additional Ground-State Results by DMRG and NQS

In the main text, we identify the phase transition points by tracking kink-like features in the evolution of S⁡(𝐊)S(\mathbf{K}) in the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases and S⁡(𝐌)S(\mathbf{M}) in the QSL and KSL phases, together with singular behavior in the entanglement entropy. Here, we provide an additional diagnostic based on the static spin structure factor, using S⁡(𝐌)S(\mathbf{M}) in the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phases and S⁡(𝐊)S(\mathbf{K}) in the QSL and KSL phases to independently cross-check the transition points. In Fig. S1(a), we show the evolution of S⁡(𝐌1)S(\mathbf{M}_{1}) and S⁡(𝐌2)S(\mathbf{M}_{2}) as a function of J2J_{2} for J1=0.5J_{1}=0.5, obtained from DMRG calculations. Two pronounced kink-like features are observed near J2≃0.35J_{2}\simeq 0.35 and 0.60.6, respectively, signaling changes in the underlying spin correlations and providing independent support for the phase boundaries shown in Figs. 3(a-c). For J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0, similar kink-like features emerge near J2≃0.86J_{2}\simeq 0.86 and 0.940.94 [cf. Fig. S1(b)]. The first kink, near J2≃0.86J_{2}\simeq 0.86, marks the transition from the (1/3,1/3)(1/3,1/3) ordered phase to the QSL phase and is also observed in the evolution of S⁡(𝐌)S(\mathbf{M}) [cf. Fig. S1(c)]. The second kink, near J2≃0.94J_{2}\simeq 0.94, agrees excellently with the QSL–KSL transition point identified from the complementary diagnostics in Figs. 3(d-f), further supporting the robustness of the phase boundaries established from our ground-state calculations.

In Fig. S2, we also present the S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) profiles obtained from NQS calculations, which are in excellent agreement with those shown in Fig. 2. One difference is that, in the QSL phase, S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) remains continuous at 𝐌2\mathbf{M}_{2}, in contrast to the behavior observed in Fig. 2(c). This difference can be attributed to the distinct cylinder and torus geometries, with the latter restoring the C3C_{3} rotational symmetry. In addition to the distinct S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) profiles shown in Figs. 2(c,d) and Figs. S2(c,d), the QSL and KSL phases can be further distinguished by their real-space spin correlations, F⁡(r)=⟨𝐒x,y⋅𝐒x+r,y⟩F(r)=\langle{{\mathbf{S}}}_{x,y}\cdot{{\mathbf{S}}}_{x+r,y}\rangle, as presented in Fig. S3. In the QSL phase [cf. Figs. S3(a-f)], F⁡(r)F(r) decays slowly and is well described by a power-law behavior, indicative of gapless excitations and consistent with the proposed Dirac QSL in the 3​J3J model. In contrast, F⁡(r)F(r) in the KSL phase [cf. Figs. S3(g-i)] decays rapidly and is well fitted by an exponential behavior, with a very short correlation length ξs∼1\xi_{\mathrm{s}}\sim 1. Here, we refrain from drawing conclusions about whether the KSL phase is gapped or gapless, as our results are only obtained from finite-size YC6 simulations, and determining the nature of the KSL in the two-dimensional limit is beyond the scope of the present work. Instead, these results provide an additional distinction between the QSL and KSL phases, without presupposing the nature of the KSL ground state.

In Fig. S4, we further examine the possibility of VBC order by calculating the nearest-neighbor bond energies. Figs. S4(a-b) show the spatial distribution of the bond energies on the YC6 kagome lattice in the QSL phase, with model parameters chosen consistently with the finite-temperature simulations. Within the present energy resolution, we find no evidence of broken lattice-translation symmetry, ruling out any discernible VBC order. Similarly, the bond energies in the KSL phase [cf. Fig. S4(d)] are highly uniform, with no discernible signature of VBC order. It is worth noting that along the diagonal line J1=J2J_{1}=J_{2}, as J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} are gradually decrease, the dominant J⎔J_{\hexagon} term leads to a characteristic spatial pattern in the bond energies, manifested as the J⎔J_{\hexagon}-dominated hexagons [green hexagons in Fig. S4(c)]. This behavior is expected, since in the limit of J1,J2→0J_{1},J_{2}\rightarrow 0, the system approaches a collection of decoupled hexagons. Importantly, however, this pattern does not break any symmetry of the 3​J3J model Hamiltonian. It merely reflects the modulation of bond energies within the unit cell and therefore does not constitute VBC order.

II NQS calculation of the ground state phase diagram

Our NQS calculations are performed on a torus of 6×66\times 6 kagome unit cells (N=3×6×6=108N=3\times 6\times 6=108 sites) with periodic boundary conditions along both lattice directions, complementing the cylindrical geometries used in our DMRG simulations. To represent the many-body wave function, we use a Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture with factored attention [99, 98, 79, 78], together with a variant described below. The two are employed in different regions of the phase diagram, according to the translation-symmetry content of the expected phases. We summarize here the main components of the original architecture and refer to Ref. [99] for a more detailed description. Both variants are illustrated in Fig. S5.

Given an input spin configuration 𝝈=(σ1z,…,σNz)\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma^{z}_{1},\ldots,\sigma^{z}_{N}) in the computational (SzS^{z}) basis, an NQS outputs the amplitude Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)=⟨𝝈|Ψ𝜽⟩∈ℂ\Psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\braket{\boldsymbol{\sigma}|\Psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\in\mathbb{C} of the variational state |Ψ𝜽⟩\ket{\Psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}, with 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} denoting the variational parameters. In the ViT of Ref. [99], the configuration is divided into n=N/Pn=N/P non-overlapping patches of PP spins. Each patch configuration 𝒑i∈{±1}P\boldsymbol{p}_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}^{P} is then mapped through a shared linear layer WW to a dd-dimensional embedding vector

𝐮i(0)=W⁡(𝒑i)≡E​𝒑i+𝐛,\mathbf{u}_{i}^{(0)}=W(\boldsymbol{p}_{i})\equiv E\,\boldsymbol{p}_{i}+\mathbf{b}, (S1)

where E∈ℝd×PE\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P} and 𝐛∈ℝd\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are learnable. The resulting sequence of embedding vectors is passed through nln_{l} transformer encoder layers implementing a factored attention mechanism with nhn_{h} heads [79, 78]. At each layer ll, every head h=1,…,nhh=1,\dots,n_{h} produces an attention vector

𝐚ih=∑j=1nwi​jh​Vh​(𝐮j(l)),\mathbf{a}^{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w^{h}_{ij}\,V^{h}(\mathbf{u}_{j}^{(l)}), (S2)

for each patch ii, where VhV^{h} is a shared linear layer from ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} to ℝd/nh\mathbb{R}^{d/n_{h}} and wi​jhw^{h}_{ij} is the factored attention weight, a learnable scalar depending only on the displacement between patches ii and jj, which renders the attention layer equivariant under patch-level translations of the input. The layer index is suppressed for all quantities other than the embedding vectors. The nhn_{h} attention vectors corresponding to patch ii are then concatenated, linearly mixed, and passed through a residual feed-forward step to produce 𝐮i(l+1)\mathbf{u}^{(l+1)}_{i} [99]. After the last encoder layer, the resulting vectors 𝐮i(nl)\mathbf{u}_{i}^{(n_{l})} are summed over the patch index and mapped to log⁡Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)\log\Psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) by a complex-valued nonlinear layer [99, 15]. This final sum-pooling promotes the translation equivariance of the embedding-encoder stack to invariance of the variational state |Ψ𝜽⟩\ket{\Psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} under patch-level translations. We use this architecture for the scan of the line J1=0.5J_{1}=0.5 in Fig. 3(b), choosing a patch of 3×33\times 3 kagome lattice unit cells (P=27P=27), which matches the magnetic unit cell of the 𝐐=(1/3,1/3)\mathbf{Q}=(1/3,1/3) ordered phase shown in the inset of Fig. 1. This inductive bias is well suited to the magnetically ordered regions, while remaining compatible with disordered states that respect a finer translation symmetry. We use nl=4n_{l}=4, d=160d=160 and nh=40n_{h}=40, corresponding to approximately 1.1×1061.1\times 10^{6} parameters.

The second architecture variant is used on the J1=1J_{1}=1 line, close to the isotropic kagome limit (J1=J2=J⎔J_{1}=J_{2}=J_{\hexagon}), where the ground state is expected to respect the translation symmetry of the 3​J3J Hamiltonian. The patches are fixed to single kagome unit cells (P=3P=3), with each patch ii being assigned a class label ci∈{0,1,2}c_{i}\in\{0,1,2\}, recording which of the three inequivalent kagome primitive cells of the nine-site 3​J3J unit cell it occupies. The embedding map and the attention weights of Eqs. (S1) and (S2) respectively are chosen to be class-dependent,

W⁡(𝒑i)→Wci​(𝒑i),wi​jh→wi​jh,ci,W(\boldsymbol{p}_{i})\to W_{c_{i}}(\boldsymbol{p}_{i}),\qquad w^{h}_{ij}\to w^{h,c_{i}}_{ij}, (S3)

replacing their shared counterparts. This change restricts the enforced translation symmetry from all kagome lattice translations, otherwise imposed by single unit cell patches, to only those of the 3​J3J Hamiltonian. In addition, given the finer patching, we adopt the spatial attenuation factor of Ref. [100], which multiplies the attention weights by a normalized exponential of the distance between patches with a learnable decay rate per layer and attention head. This introduces a locality inductive bias, which can be lifted or strengthened through optimization. We use nl=8n_{l}=8, d=72d=72 and nh=12n_{h}=12, corresponding to approximately 4.4×1054.4\times 10^{5} parameters.

For every point (J1,J2)(J_{1},J_{2}) of the two scans, the ViT parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} are optimized by minimizing the variational energy within the variational Monte Carlo framework [9]. Since the Hamiltonian (1) commutes with Stotz=∑iSizS^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}, we perform Monte Carlo sampling within the Stotz=0S^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}=0 sector using update proposals that exchange pairs of opposite spins. We minimize the energy over 10410^{4} steps with M=8192M=8192 samples per step, using the Subsampled Projected-Increment Natural Gradient Descent (SPRING) optimization algorithm [31], which builds upon the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [92, 5] and MinSR [17, 81] schemes, with momentum μ=0.9\mu=0.9 and a cosine-decaying [68, 21] learning rate from 2×10−22\times 10^{-2} to 10−310^{-3}. The diagonal shift regularization is held constant at λ=10−4\lambda=10^{-4} for the first variant, while for the second variant it is cosine decayed from 10−310^{-3} to 10−410^{-4} over the run, to stabilize the early optimization of the deeper network. After optimization, the static spin structure factor shown in Figs. 3 (b,e) and S2 are estimated with 2162^{16} Monte Carlo samples drawn from the final state. All NQS simulations are performed using NetKet [14, 97], which is built on top of the JAX [10] and Flax [39] libraries.

III Thermal tensor network calculation of the specific heat

III.1 exponential tensor renormalization group

The exponential tensor renormalization group (XTRG) method starts by constructing the high‑temperature density operator ρ^​(τ)=e−τ​H\hat{\rho}(\tau)=e^{-\tau H}, where τ\tau denotes an infinitesimally small inverse temperature. This initial state can be reliably obtained via the Trotter–Suzuki decomposition [96, 95] or through series‑expansion techniques [19]. A central ingredient of XTRG is its exponential evolution scheme: the density operator is repeatedly squared, i.e., ρ^n+1=ρ^n⋅ρ^n\hat{\rho}_{n+1}=\hat{\rho}_{n}\cdot\hat{\rho}_{n}, which doubles the inverse temperature at each step. This exponential growth drastically reduces the number of imaginary‑time evolution and truncation steps, thereby enabling accurate simulations down to very low temperatures. In practice, we begin at a tiny inverse temperature τ0\tau_{0} on the order of ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4} using the series‑expansion method:

ρ^0≡ρ^​(τ0)≃∑k=0𝒩c(−τ0)kk!​Hk,\hat{\rho}_{0}\equiv\hat{\rho}(\tau_{0})\simeq\sum_{k=0}^{\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{c}}}\frac{(-\tau_{0})^{k}}{k!}H^{k},

with a truncated expansion order 𝒩c=4\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{c}}=4. We then apply the squaring procedure 19 times to access the lowest temperatures, enabling accurate temperature measurements down to T∼0.05​J⎔T\sim 0.05J_{\hexagon}.

In Fig. S6, we present the specific heat at several J2J_{2} values computed from XTRG with D=1000D=1000, for the benefit of interested readers. The energy scale is set to J⎔=1J_{\hexagon}=1. From the Cv​(T)C_{v}(T) curves, distinct features of the ordered and QSL phases are clearly visible for both J1=0.8J_{1}=0.8 and J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0. The ordered phase is characterized by a pronounced peak near T≈1T\approx 1, which gradually diminishes as the system enters the QSL phase. Concurrently, a shoulder-like feature emerges at T≈0.1T\approx 0.1 within the QSL phase.

III.2 tangent-space tensor renormalization group

We also employ the tangent-space tensor renormalization group (tanTRG) method as another self-consistent computation at intermediate temperatures. The simulation procedure also begins by representing the spin Hamiltonian as an MPO, and the thermal density operator ρ⁡(β)=e−β​H\rho(\beta)=e^{-\beta H} is initialized at an infinite-temperature limit (small inverse temperature β=0\beta=0), providing an accurate starting point for the imaginary-time evolution. The cooling process to lower temperatures is then governed by the flow equation d​ρ/d​β=−H​ρd\rho/d\beta=-H\rho. To maintain computational efficiency within a manageable bond dimension DD, the evolution is restricted to the MPO manifold by projecting the right-hand side onto the tangent space at the current state, expressed as d​ρ/d​β=𝒫⁡(−H​ρ)d\rho/d\beta=\mathcal{P}(-H\rho), where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the tangent-space projector. Throughout the evolution, thermodynamic observables such as the free energy, internal energy, and specific heat are directly evaluated from the MPO representation of the density operator at each temperature step. Practically, we chose a we impose SU(2) symmetry with D=1000∼2000D=1000\sim 2000 U(1) states retained, achieving a peak truncation error of roughly 10−410^{-4} across the temperature range extending to T∼0.08T\sim 0.08.

Moreover, Fig. S7 compares XTRG and tanTRG calculations at (J1,J2)=(1.0,0.9)​J⎔(J_{1},J_{2})=(1.0,0.9)J_{\hexagon} with bond dimensions increasing from 10001000 to 15001500 to 20002000. The XTRG results converge well and show little dependence on bond dimension, whereas the tanTRG results exhibit a noticeable variation. Combined with Fig. 5, the tanTRG results gradually approach the XTRG ones, particularly at low temperatures (T/J⎔<0.5T/J_{\hexagon}<0.5). This behavior indicates that XTRG outperforms tanTRG in the low-temperature regime.
